finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token with PHP loose == against the caller-supplied token. A non-string value such as JSON boolean true matches any non-empty stored token, so an attacker can reset the password of any account that has an outstanding reset row without knowing the token. Under PHP < 8, integer 0 also matches non-numeric strings.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (reset.php:2). Attacker-controlled if the caller passes a typed JSON value. Precondition: a resets row exists for the victim email, which happens when the victim has requested a reset.
finding.sink: reset.php:5-6 UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ...

trace.note: Loads stored token by email using PDO quote. The email path is not SQL-injectable.
$row['token'] == $token uses loose comparison; 'abc' == true is true in PHP.
Password is replaced with the attacker's hash for the victim email.

finding.guards_checked: Email is parameterized via PDO quote, so no SQLi. Row existence is required. No type check and no strict comparison. No caller or entry point is in the repo, so reachability is unverified; severity depends on whether a typed JSON body reaches this function.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:4 uses loose `==` with no type check, and nothing in the repo checks the return value of reset_password_loose. reset.php:14 (reset_password) uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but that is a different function and is not on this path.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: reset.php:3 loads the stored token via $db->quote, reset.php:4 compares with loose `==`, and reset.php:5-6 overwrites the password, and PHP's `'abc' == true` behaves as claimed. The repo contains only reset.php with no caller or HTTP entry point, so I cannot tell whether an attacker can pass a JSON boolean into $token, which decides whether this is exploitable; the sibling reset_password at reset.php:12-20 may suggest this function is legacy or unused, which would need checking.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never consumed or expiry-checked. The resets row is not deleted or marked used after a successful reset, and neither function checks an expiry. A token that was used or leaked stays valid for repeated resets.
finding.source: Any holder of a previously issued reset token for the email, e.g. from an email link, proxy log, or Referer leak, used before or after the legitimate reset.

trace.note: Fetches the single resets row for the email with no expires_at or used filter.
hash_equals validates the token, but nothing invalidates it.
Password is updated and the function returns true, leaving the row intact.

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals is constant-time. The schema is not in the repo, so an expires_at column or a delete elsewhere cannot be ruled out. Severity is PLAUSIBLE pending the schema and the code that issues tokens.

verdict.guard_found: none in the repo. The only code is reset.php (two functions). hash_equals at reset.php:14 is a constant-time comparison, not an expiry or consumption check. Nothing in the repo issues tokens, deletes rows, or defines the resets schema, so a DELETE, an expires_at column, or a trigger elsewhere cannot be ruled out.
verdict.reason: Lines reset.php:13-16 match the trace: the resets row is read with no expiry or used filter, and it is never deleted or marked used, so the token survives the reset (reset.php:14-17). Whether that is exploitable depends on code outside the repo (the resets schema, token issuance, and any cleanup or caller), and none of it is present, so the verdict cannot be decided from the available code.

finding.claim: If resets.token is NULL or empty and the caller submits an empty token, hash_equals('', '') succeeds and the password is reset without a valid token.
finding.source: Caller-supplied empty $token for an email whose resets row has a NULL or empty token. Precondition: such a row can be created.

trace.note: Fetches the row, including a NULL or empty token value.
hash_equals coerces NULL to '' and compares it with (string)'' = ''. Returns true.

finding.guards_checked: Row existence is required. No non-empty check on $token or the stored value. Whether empty tokens can be stored depends on the issuing code, which is not in the repo. Severity is LOW and speculative.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is row existence at reset.php:14 (`$row &&`). Nothing rejects an empty $token or an empty/NULL stored token. The `$token` argument is cast with (string) at line 14, which does not block it.
verdict.reason: The trace at reset.php:13-16 is accurate: hash_equals(null→'', (string)'') returns true, so reset_password (reset.php:14-16) runs when both values are empty. Whether a resets row with a NULL or empty token can exist depends on the code that inserts rows, and that code is not in this directory (the only file is reset.php), so the precondition cannot be decided here.
